claims.text: Ultra-thin layer architectures in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings inhibit time-dependent plastic deformation through geometric confinement of dislocations.
Geometric confinement limits dislocation nucleation in ultra-thin multilayers.
Geometric confinement limits dislocation glide in ultra-thin multilayers.
Geometric confinement limits dislocation climb in ultra-thin multilayers.
Ultra-thin layers create confined microstructural domains that restrict the space available for dislocation propagation.
Restricting dislocation interactions reduces dislocation-mediated plastic flow.
Confinement enhances creep resistance by limiting the accumulation of plastic strain over time.
At 0.3–0.4 Tm, dislocation motion is active in the proposed multilayer coatings.
Interface diffusion remains minimal at 0.3–0.4 Tm in the proposed multilayer coatings.
A coating with 5 nm layers will have significantly less creep strain than an otherwise comparable coating with 50 nm layers.
A coating with 5 nm layers will exhibit lower dislocation mobility than an otherwise comparable coating with 50 nm layers.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity is less geometrically constrained in 50 nm layers than in 5 nm layers.
The proposed mechanism applies when dislocation-mediated deformation dominates at moderate homologous temperatures and stresses.
At very high temperatures, interface diffusion can mask the geometric-confinement effect.
Under extreme loading, additional deformation mechanisms can mask the geometric-confinement effect.
Interface diffusion, residual stresses, and other microstructural phenomena may complicate attribution of creep resistance to geometric confinement.

contradictions.description: The coatings are described as having the same or consistent architecture while individual layer thickness—an architectural parameter—is deliberately varied. The intended meaning appears to be that all architectural features except layer thickness are held constant.
